newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sunni-Shi'ite tension flares in Pakistan, India.
newsitem.headline: Sunni-Shi'ite tension flares in Pakistan, India.

text.p: Feuding among militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslems poses a tough challenge to Pakistan's new government, while Sunni-Shi'ite tensions have resurfaced in neighbouring India, sparking unrest in the city of Lucknow.
A deadly cycle of revenge killings has cost more than 110 lives in Pakistan this year, with fresh murders almost daily.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government has had scant success in curbing the gunmen since taking power in February.
The vendetta is being fought mainly in the populous central province of Punjab, where the chief minister, Sharif's younger brother Shahbaz, vowed this week to focus on halting it.
"He has made similar statements in the recent past, which are bound to prove somewhat embarrassing for him in the light of continuing violence," the Lahore-based daily Nation commented.
A Punjab police spokesman said police were ill-equipped to deal with the well-armed gunmen, so the provincial government had asked for 432 army officers to be loaned to train them.
He accused Koranic schools of turning out extremists.

"There are over 200 madrasas which are virtually machines for inducting fanatics into society," he said. "These fanatics are recruited to military training camps in various parts of the country for the cause of holy war in Afghanistan and Kashmir."
Police sources said the Shi'ite Sipah-i-Mohammad Pakistan group had reorganised in May and was ready to take on Sunni rivals such as Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan and Lashkar-i-Jhangvi.

Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's mostly Sunni population of 138 million. India's smaller Shi'ite community is concentrated in just four districts, including Lucknow, in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh.

In Lucknow, where last month's clashes with Moslem marchers prompted police to enforce an indefinite curfew and detain hundreds of people, Shi'ites account for about a quarter of the 600,000 Moslems among the city's two million people.
The violence erupted on June 26 when some 15,000 Shi'ites defied a 20-year-old ban on religious processions, imposed in 1977 after about 15 people were killed in communal clashes.

Police in New Delhi used water cannons on Monday to disperse Shi'ites protesting at the arrest of Shi'ite leader Maulana Kalbe Jawwad, who has campaigned to end the ban on marches to mark the death of Prophet Mohammed's grandson Hussain.
Communal tension in Lucknow dates back to the 18th century, when ruling Shi'ite Nawabs barred Sunnis from observing certain rituals, but allowed Shi'ites their mourning ceremonies.
Periodic riots occurred during British rule in 1888, 1906 and 1939 and after independence in 1969, 1974 and 1977.

Indian historian Mashirul Hasan said the latest trouble followed a similar pattern to previous riots, with the government "playing much the same partisan role" as in 1939, when the state banned Shi'ite mourning processions.
"Traditionally in Uttar Pradesh, Shi'ites and Sunnis are pawns on the chessboard of local provincial politics," he said.

"Part of the animus is because Lucknow is the biggest concentration of orthodox Sunni and orthodox Shi'ite organisations...which are old, connected with established families and have a popular base," Hasan told Reuters.

He said relatively poor Shi'ites lived cheek by jowl with wealthier Sunnis in the Old City of Lucknow. "When you live together and see your neighbour doing rather well, it invites jealousy and hostility, and if on top of that ideological nuances are introduced, then they blow up," he said.
The same doctrinal disputes that have divided Sunnis and Shi'ites since the dawn of Islam are still a source of tension.
But in Pakistan, religious divisions have degenerated into a brutal feud which mainstream Sunni and Shi'ite clerics are quick to disavow and condemn as a threat to Moslem harmony.
Allama Syed Iftikhar Hussain Naqvi, central secretary general of the Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan movement, said Indian or Israeli secret services could be behind the violence.
"None of this violence has any link with sectarian differences between Moslems nor is any sectarian group or party ready to support or patronise this kind of terrorism," he said.

"The involvement of certain foreign agencies including (India's Research and Analysis Wing) RAW and (Israel's) Mossad cannot be ruled out. These agencies are supporting terrorism to weaken Pakistan and malign Islam internationally. "Certain elements in Pakistan have been playing into their hands and have become their tool," Naqvi declared.

He criticised this week's crackdown in which police have rounded up scores of religious party activists and leaders, saying it was targeting the wrong people and was liable to backfire against Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League government.
Iran and Saudi Arabia are widely believed to use Pakistan as a proxy battleground, with Tehran sponsoring Shi'ite militants and Riyadh their Sunni counterparts. Both countries deny it.
Pakistani militants can easily acquire assault rifles and other weapons from supplies that flooded into the country in the 1980s intended for Afghan guerrillas fighting Soviet troops.
